topics.title: The Verb 'To Be'
topics.summary: am, is, are: saying who you are, where you are and how you feel.
topics.explanation:
'To be' is the most important verb in English.
I am · you are · he/she/it is · we are · they are.
Short forms (contractions) are normal in speech: I'm, you're, he's, she's, it's, we're, they're.
Negative: add 'not': I'm not, he isn't (is not), they aren't (are not).
Questions: put the verb first: 'Are you a student?' 'Is she from Toronto?' Short answers: 'Yes, I am.' 'No, she isn't.'
French speakers: age uses 'to be', not 'have': 'I am 30' (NOT *I have 30 years). Also: 'I am hungry / cold / right / afraid' (j'ai faim / froid / raison / peur).
topics.explanation_fr: Âge, faim, froid, raison, peur : on utilise 'to be' en anglais. « J'ai 30 ans » = I am 30.

examples.en: I'm Arnaud. I'm from Montréal.
She isn't at home. She's at work.
Are they your colleagues? — Yes, they are.
I'm 35 years old.

exercises.prompt: My brother ___ a teacher.
___ you from Canada?
We ___ (not) tired. (use the short form)
answer: aren't
are not
're not

exercises.prompt: I have 28 years.
answer: I am 28 years old.
I'm 28 years old.
I am 28.

exercises.prompt: Traduisez : « J'ai froid. »
answer: I am cold.
I'm cold.

topics.title: Present Simple
topics.summary: Habits, routines and facts: I work, she works.
topics.explanation:
Use the present simple for habits, routines, timetables and things that are always true: 'I drink coffee every morning.' 'Water boils at 100 °C.'
Form: I/you/we/they work · he/she/it works (add -s). Spelling: watch → watches, study → studies, go → goes, have → has.
Negative: don't / doesn't + base verb: 'She doesn't work on Fridays' (NOT *doesn't works).
Questions: Do / Does + subject + base verb: 'Do you speak French?' 'Where does he live?'
Common time words: always, usually, often, sometimes, never, every day, on Mondays. Frequency adverbs go before the main verb: 'I usually take the bus.'
topics.explanation_fr: N'oubliez pas le -s à la 3e personne : she works. Après does/doesn't, le verbe reste à la base : Does she work?

examples.en: I start work at nine.
He lives in Ottawa and works in a bank.
We don't watch TV in the evening.
Does she speak English? — Yes, she does.

exercises.prompt: My sister ___ in a hospital.
___ you like coffee?
He ___ (not / eat) meat.
answer: doesn't eat
does not eat

exercises.prompt: She don't like Mondays.
answer: She doesn't like Mondays.
She does not like Mondays.

exercises.prompt: Choose the correct word order:

topics.title: Present Continuous
topics.summary: What is happening now: I'm reading, they're working.
topics.explanation:
Use the present continuous for actions happening now or around now: 'I'm cooking dinner.' 'She's studying English this year.'
Form: am/is/are + verb-ing. Spelling: make → making, run → running, sit → sitting.
Negative: 'He isn't listening.' Questions: 'Are you working today?' 'What are you doing?'
Present simple vs continuous: habits → simple ('I usually walk'), now → continuous ('Today I'm taking the bus').
Some verbs are rarely continuous (state verbs): like, love, know, want, need, understand: 'I know' (NOT *I'm knowing).
topics.explanation_fr: Pas de forme « en train de » en français standard : I'm working = je travaille (en ce moment). Les verbes d'état (know, want, like) restent au présent simple.

examples.en: Look! It's snowing.
I'm reading a great book at the moment.
What are you doing? — I'm making coffee.
I want a coffee. (NOT I'm wanting)

exercises.prompt: Be quiet! The baby ___.
They ___ (watch) a film right now.
answer: are watching
're watching

exercises.prompt: I ___ what you mean.
She is work at the moment.
answer: She is working at the moment.
She's working at the moment.

exercises.prompt: He usually ___ to work, but today he ___ the bus.

topics.title: Asking Questions
topics.summary: Yes/no questions and question words: what, where, when, who, how.
topics.explanation:
Yes/no questions: with 'to be', invert: 'Is he here?'. With other verbs, use do/does: 'Do you work here?'
Question words: what (thing), where (place), when (time), who (person), why (reason), how (manner), how much (price/uncountable), how many (countable), how old (age), what time.
Word order: question word + do/does/be + subject + verb: 'Where do you live?' 'What time does the train leave?' 'How old are you?'
French speakers: don't forget do/does: *Where you live? → Where do you live?
topics.explanation_fr: N'oubliez pas l'auxiliaire do/does : « Où habites-tu ? » = Where do you live?

examples.en: Where do you work?
What time is it?
How much is this coffee?
Who is your teacher?

exercises.prompt: ___ do you live? — In Québec City.
___ is the meeting? — At 3 p.m.
Where you work?
answer: Where do you work?

exercises.prompt: How ___ brothers do you have? (many/much)
answer: many

exercises.prompt: ___ she speak Spanish?

topics.title: Building Basic Sentences
topics.summary: Subject + verb + object, adjectives before nouns, and where to put place and time.
topics.explanation:
English word order is fixed: Subject + Verb + Object: 'Marie drinks tea.'
Adjectives go before the noun and never take -s: 'a red car', 'two red cars' (NOT *a car red, *reds cars).
Place before time at the end: 'I go to the gym every day.' 'We met in Paris last year.'
Every sentence needs a subject: 'It is raining.' 'It's late.' (NOT *Is raining).
There is / there are to say something exists: 'There is a café near my office.' 'There are three people in the room.'
topics.explanation_fr: L'adjectif se place avant le nom et reste invariable : « des voitures rouges » = red cars. « Il y a » = there is / there are.

examples.en: I have a small apartment.
She works in Toronto every summer.
There are two banks on this street.
It's cold today.

exercises.prompt: Choose the correct sentence:
___ a supermarket near here?
Is very hot today.
answer: It is very hot today.
It's very hot today.

exercises.prompt: We go every Sunday to the market.
answer: We go to the market every Sunday.

exercises.prompt: Traduisez : « Il y a trois chambres dans la maison. »
answer: There are three bedrooms in the house.
There are three rooms in the house.
exercises.explanation: Il y a + pluriel = there are.

topics.title: Past Simple
topics.summary: Finished actions in the past: worked, went, saw, did.
topics.explanation:
Use the past simple for finished actions at a finished time: yesterday, last week, in 2020, two days ago.
Regular verbs: add -ed: work → worked, live → lived, study → studied, stop → stopped.
Irregular verbs must be learned: go → went, have → had, see → saw, make → made, get → got, take → took, buy → bought, say → said, come → came, be → was/were.
Negative: didn't + base verb: 'I didn't go' (NOT *didn't went). Questions: Did + subject + base verb: 'Did you see it?' 'Where did you go?'
topics.explanation_fr: Après did/didn't, le verbe reste à la base : Did you go? I didn't go. « Il y a deux jours » = two days ago.

examples.en: I visited my parents last weekend.
We went to Vancouver in 2022.
She didn't call me yesterday.
What did you do on Saturday?

exercises.prompt: Yesterday I ___ a new phone.
They ___ (not / come) to the party.
answer: didn't come
did not come

exercises.prompt: Did you went to the meeting?
answer: Did you go to the meeting?

exercises.prompt: I moved to Canada three years ___.
Where ___ you have lunch yesterday?
answer: did

topics.title: Talking About the Future: going to and will
topics.summary: Plans with 'going to', quick decisions and promises with 'will'.
topics.explanation:
going to + verb: plans and intentions already decided: 'I'm going to visit my sister next month.'
Also predictions from what we can see: 'Look at the sky. It's going to rain.'
will + verb: decisions made now, offers, promises: 'I'll help you.' 'I'll call you tonight.'
Also general predictions and opinions: 'I think it will be a good year.'
Negative: won't (will not), isn't going to. Questions: 'Will you come?' 'Are you going to apply?'
Present continuous for fixed arrangements: 'I'm meeting Tom at six.'
topics.explanation_fr: « Je vais » (projet) = I'm going to. Décision spontanée ou promesse = I'll.

examples.en: We're going to buy a house next year.
The phone is ringing. — I'll answer it.
I think you'll love Montréal.
I won't be late, I promise.

exercises.prompt: I've decided. I ___ learn to drive this summer.
It's hot in here. — I ___ open the window.
Don't worry, I ___ (not) tell anyone. (short form)
answer: won't
will not

exercises.prompt: Tomorrow I will to go to the bank.
answer: Tomorrow I will go to the bank.
Tomorrow I'm going to go to the bank.
Tomorrow I am going to go to the bank.
Tomorrow I'm going to the bank.

topics.title: Comparatives and Superlatives
topics.summary: bigger, more expensive, the best: comparing people, places and things.
topics.explanation:
Short adjectives (1 syllable): add -er / -est: cheap → cheaper → the cheapest; big → bigger → the biggest.
Adjectives ending in -y: easy → easier → the easiest.
Long adjectives (2+ syllables): more / the most: expensive → more expensive → the most expensive.
Irregular: good → better → the best; bad → worse → the worst; far → farther/further → the farthest.
Use 'than' with comparatives: 'Toronto is bigger than Ottawa.' (NOT *more big, *bigger that).
as … as for equality: 'This phone is as fast as that one.' 'It isn't as cheap as I thought.'
topics.explanation_fr: « Plus grand que » = bigger than (jamais *more big). « Le meilleur » = the best.

examples.en: This hotel is cheaper than that one.
It's the most beautiful city in Canada.
My English is better than last year.
The test wasn't as difficult as I expected.

exercises.prompt: A plane is ___ than a train.
This is ___ restaurant in town.
Montréal is more big than Québec City.
answer: Montréal is bigger than Québec City.
Montreal is bigger than Quebec City.

exercises.prompt: Learning English is ___ (easy) than learning Mandarin.
answer: easier

exercises.prompt: This laptop is ___ expensive ___ the other one. (equality)
answer: as/as
as as
as, as

topics.title: Modal Verbs: can, must, have to, should
topics.summary: Ability, permission, obligation and advice.
topics.explanation:
can / can't: ability and permission: 'I can swim.' 'Can I sit here?'
must / have to: obligation. 'You must wear a helmet.' (rule) 'I have to work on Saturday.' (external obligation).
don't have to = not necessary: 'You don't have to come.' mustn't = not allowed: 'You mustn't smoke here.'
should / shouldn't: advice: 'You should see a doctor.'
Modals have no -s and are followed by the base verb without 'to': 'She can drive' (NOT *She cans, *can to drive). Exception: have to.
topics.explanation_fr: « Tu ne dois pas » (interdiction) = you mustn't ; « tu n'es pas obligé » = you don't have to. Pas de 'to' après can/must/should.

examples.en: Can you help me with this form?
You don't have to pay; it's free.
You mustn't park here.
You should practise every day.

exercises.prompt: It's a free event. You ___ buy a ticket.
She ___ speak three languages.
You should to rest.
answer: You should rest.

exercises.prompt: Passengers ___ use phones during take-off. It's not allowed.
Traduisez : « Tu devrais apprendre l'anglais. »
answer: You should learn English.

topics.title: Past Perfect
topics.summary: had + past participle: what happened before another past event.
topics.explanation:
Use the past perfect to show that one past action happened before another past action or time: 'When I arrived, the meeting had already started.'
Form: had + past participle: had gone, had finished, had seen. Short form: I'd, she'd.
Compare: 'When I arrived, the meeting started' (it started as I arrived) vs 'had started' (it started before).
Common with: already, just, never…before, by the time, after, before.
Don't overuse it: if the order is clear (with before/after), the past simple is often fine: 'I left after I finished' is acceptable.
topics.explanation_fr: Équivalent du plus-que-parfait : « J'avais déjà mangé » = I had already eaten.

examples.en: By the time we got to the station, the train had left.
She had never seen snow before she moved to Canada.
I'd just finished the report when my boss called.
They were tired because they had worked all night.

exercises.prompt: When I got home, someone ___ the window.
She ___ (never / fly) before her trip to Paris.
answer: had never flown

exercises.prompt: When we arrived, the film has already started.
answer: When we arrived, the film had already started.

exercises.prompt: Traduisez : « Il avait déjà payé l'addition. »
answer: He had already paid the bill.
He'd already paid the bill.
He had already paid the check.

topics.title: Phrasal Verbs: Meaning and Word Order
topics.summary: look after, give up, find out, turn down — and where the object goes.
topics.explanation:
A phrasal verb = verb + particle (up, out, off, on, down…). The meaning is often not obvious: give up = stop trying; find out = discover; look after = take care of; turn down = refuse; run out of = have no more; get on with = have a good relationship.
Separable phrasal verbs: a noun object can go before or after the particle: 'turn off the light' / 'turn the light off'. A pronoun MUST go in the middle: 'turn it off' (NOT *turn off it).
Inseparable: the object always goes after: 'look after the children', 'look after them'.
Three-part verbs are inseparable: 'I ran out of time', 'She gets on with her colleagues'.
topics.explanation_fr: Avec un pronom, la particule va à la fin : « Éteins-la » = turn it off.

examples.en: I gave up smoking two years ago.
Can you pick me up at the station?
We've run out of milk.
I need to find out what time the store opens.

exercises.prompt: The company offered her a job, but she ___ it ___.
Please turn off it.
answer: Please turn it off.

exercises.prompt: Who will ___ your dog while you're away?
We ran ___ of paper, so I couldn't print the report.
answer: out

exercises.prompt: I need to ___ how much the course costs.

topics.title: Narrative Tenses for Storytelling
topics.summary: Past continuous, past simple and past perfect working together in a story.
topics.explanation:
Good stories combine three past tenses:
Past continuous (was/were + -ing) sets the scene or describes an action in progress: 'It was raining and people were hurrying home.'
Past simple gives the main events in order: 'Suddenly, the lights went out.'
Past perfect goes back to an earlier event: 'I realised I had left my keys at the office.'
'When' + past simple often interrupts a continuous action: 'I was cooking when the phone rang.' 'While' + continuous for two simultaneous actions: 'While I was waiting, I read the news.'
topics.explanation_fr: Imparfait (décor, action en cours) ≈ past continuous ; passé composé/simple (événements) ≈ past simple ; plus-que-parfait ≈ past perfect.

examples.en: I was walking to work when I saw an old friend.
While she was talking, everyone was taking notes.
When I got to the airport, I realised I had forgotten my passport.
The sun was shining, and the streets were full of tourists.

exercises.prompt: I ___ a shower when the doorbell rang.
While we ___ dinner, the power went off.
She was upset because she ___ (lose) her phone earlier that day.
answer: had lost

exercises.prompt: When I was arriving, they already left.
answer: When I arrived, they had already left.
exercises.explanation: Arrival = event (past simple); leaving happened before (past perfect).

topics.title: Present Perfect vs Past Simple
topics.summary: Choose between a finished past time and a connection to the present.
topics.explanation:
Use the past simple for actions completed at a specific, finished time (yesterday, in 2019, last week, when I was a student). Use the present perfect (have/has + past participle) when the time is unfinished or unspecified and the result or experience matters now (today, this year, ever, never, already, yet, so far, since, for).

French speakers often use the past simple where English needs the present perfect with 'since/for': French 'J'habite ici depuis 2015' is 'I have lived here since 2015', not '*I live here since 2015'.

A time expression that refers to a finished period forces the past simple: '*I have seen him yesterday' is wrong.
topics.explanation_fr: Le past simple situe l'action dans un passé terminé et daté. Le present perfect relie le passé au présent (expérience, résultat, période non terminée). Attention : « depuis » se traduit par le present perfect + since/for.

examples.en: I have worked at the bank since 2018.
examples.note: Still working there: present perfect + since.

examples.en: I worked at the bank from 2015 to 2018.
Have you ever presented to a board of directors?
Our revenue has grown by 12% this quarter.
The market crashed in March.

exercises.prompt: I ___ in Montréal for ten years, and I still love it.
exercises.explanation: Situation continuing to now + 'for ten years' → present perfect.

exercises.prompt: She ___ the report yesterday afternoon.
exercises.explanation: 'Yesterday afternoon' is a finished time → past simple.

exercises.prompt: We ___ (not / receive) the invoice yet.
answer: haven't received
have not received

exercises.prompt: I know him since we were at university.
answer: I have known him since we were at university.
I've known him since we were at university.
exercises.explanation: State continuing to now with 'since' → present perfect (know is stative, so not continuous).

exercises.prompt: Did you ever visit Vancouver?
answer: Have you ever visited Vancouver?
exercises.explanation: 'Ever' asking about life experience → present perfect.

exercises.prompt: Traduisez : « Je travaille sur ce projet depuis trois mois. »
answer: I have been working on this project for three months.
I've been working on this project for three months.
I have worked on this project for three months.
I've worked on this project for three months.

topics.title: Conditionals: Zero to Mixed
topics.summary: Real, hypothetical and past-unreal conditions, plus mixed time references.
topics.explanation:
Zero: if + present, present — general truths. 'If interest rates rise, bond prices fall.'
First: if + present, will — likely future. 'If we sign today, we'll start on Monday.'
Second: if + past, would — unreal present/future. 'If I had more time, I would study law.'
Third: if + past perfect, would have + past participle — unreal past. 'If we had hedged, we wouldn't have lost money.'
Mixed: past condition → present result: 'If I had taken that job, I would be in Toronto now.' Present condition → past result: 'If I weren't so cautious, I would have invested earlier.'

Never put 'will' or 'would' in the if-clause (except for polite requests: 'If you would follow me…'). French speakers often write '*If I would have known' — the correct form is 'If I had known'.
topics.explanation_fr: Jamais de « would » dans la proposition en « if » : « Si j'avais su » = « If I had known ». Les conditionnels mixtes croisent passé et présent.

examples.en: If you heat ice, it melts.
If the client agrees, we'll send the contract tomorrow.
If I were you, I would negotiate a higher salary.
examples.note: Second conditional; 'were' for all persons in formal English.

examples.en: If they had read the terms, they wouldn't have signed.
If I had studied finance, I would be an analyst now.

exercises.prompt: If I ___ about the meeting, I would have come.
If she hadn't missed the flight, she ___ here now.
exercises.explanation: Mixed conditional: past condition, present result ('now').

exercises.prompt: If the price ___ (drop) below $50, we will buy more shares.
answer: drops

exercises.prompt: If I would have more money, I would travel.
answer: If I had more money, I would travel.
If I had more money, I'd travel.
exercises.explanation: No 'would' in the if-clause; second conditional uses past simple.

exercises.prompt: If we would have invested earlier, we would have made a profit.
answer: If we had invested earlier, we would have made a profit.
If we'd invested earlier, we would have made a profit.
If we'd invested earlier, we'd have made a profit.

topics.title: Inversion for Emphasis
topics.summary: Front negative adverbials and invert subject and auxiliary for formal emphasis.
topics.explanation:
After certain negative or restrictive adverbials placed at the start of a clause, English inverts the subject and auxiliary, as in a question: Never, Rarely, Seldom, Hardly…when, No sooner…than, Not only…but also, Only then, Only after, Under no circumstances, At no time, Little (did I know).

'Never have I seen such volatility.' 'Not only did the company miss its targets, but it also lost its CEO.'

If there is no auxiliary, add do/does/did. With 'Only after/when/if', inversion happens in the main clause: 'Only after the audit did we discover the error.'

Inverted conditionals drop 'if': 'Had we known…' (= If we had known), 'Should you need help…' (= If you need help), 'Were the rates to rise…'. These are very common in formal business writing.
topics.explanation_fr: Comme en interrogative : auxiliaire avant le sujet après un adverbe négatif placé en tête. Registre soutenu, très utile à l'écrit (IELTS, rapports).

examples.en: Rarely do we see such strong quarterly growth.
No sooner had the market opened than prices plunged.
Under no circumstances should you share your password.
Had I known about the merger, I would have sold my shares.
Should you have any questions, please do not hesitate to contact me.
examples.note: Inverted first conditional, classic email closing.

exercises.prompt: Not only ___ the deadline, but they also exceeded the budget.
Hardly ___ sat down when the phone rang.
exercises.explanation: Hardly + had + subject + past participle … when.

exercises.prompt: ___ you require further information, please contact our office. (formal 'If')
answer: Should

exercises.prompt: Never I have seen such a well-organised conference.
answer: Never have I seen such a well-organised conference.
Never have I seen such a well-organized conference.

exercises.prompt: Only after the meeting we understood the problem.
answer: Only after the meeting did we understand the problem.
exercises.explanation: Only after + noun phrase → inversion in the main clause with did.

exercises.prompt: Rewrite formally with inversion: 'If we had known about the risks, we would not have invested.'
answer: Had we known about the risks, we would not have invested.
Had we known about the risks, we wouldn't have invested.
exercises.explanation: Drop 'if' and invert: Had + subject + past participle.

topics.title: The Passive Voice in Professional English
topics.summary: Form the passive in all tenses and use it to focus on actions, results and processes.
topics.explanation:
Form: be (in the right tense) + past participle. 'The report is reviewed / was reviewed / has been reviewed / will be reviewed / is being reviewed.'

Use it when the agent is unknown, obvious or unimportant, or to sound objective: 'Mistakes were made.' 'The data were collected over six months.'

Reporting passives are common in news and academic English: 'It is believed that…', 'The company is said to be considering a sale.', 'Prices are expected to rise.'

'Have/get something done' (causative): 'We had the contract reviewed by a lawyer.'

Avoid overusing the passive in emails: active is often clearer and more direct.
topics.explanation_fr: Être + participe passé. Le passif « impersonnel » (It is believed that…) correspond souvent au « on » français : « On dit que… » = « It is said that… ».

examples.en: The new policy will be implemented in January.
Your application is being processed.
The bank is reported to have lost $2 billion.
We need to get the software updated.

exercises.prompt: The results ___ next week.
exercises.explanation: Future passive: will be + past participle.

exercises.prompt: The building ___ (renovate) at the moment, so the office is closed.
answer: is being renovated

exercises.prompt: Traduisez : « On pense que l'économie va ralentir. »
answer: It is thought that the economy will slow down.
It is believed that the economy will slow down.
The economy is thought to be slowing down.
The economy is expected to slow down.
It is thought that the economy is going to slow down.

exercises.prompt: The meeting was took place in Ottawa.
answer: The meeting took place in Ottawa.
The meeting was held in Ottawa.
exercises.explanation: 'Take place' is intransitive and has no passive; or use 'was held'.

topics.title: Articles: a, an, the, or nothing
topics.summary: The zero article is where French speakers struggle most.
topics.explanation:
Use 'a/an' for one non-specific countable thing: 'She's an economist.' (Note: jobs take an article in English, unlike French 'Elle est économiste'.)
Use 'the' when both speakers know which one: 'The meeting starts at 3.'
Use NO article for general statements with plural or uncountable nouns: 'Inflation affects everyone.' 'Banks need capital.' French uses 'le/la/les' here ('L'inflation touche tout le monde'), so French speakers often add a wrong 'the'.

No article with most names of countries, companies, meals, and with 'next/last + time': 'next week', 'in Canada', 'at lunch'. But: the United States, the UK, the Netherlands.
topics.explanation_fr: Les généralités en anglais n'ont pas d'article : « La finance est complexe » = « Finance is complex ». Les métiers prennent « a/an ».

examples.en: Education is the key to success.
The education I received in Lyon was excellent.
He works as a data scientist.
I'll see you next Monday.

exercises.prompt: ___ unemployment has fallen in most provinces.
My sister is engineer at the Hydro-Québec.
answer: My sister is an engineer at Hydro-Québec.
My sister is an engineer at Hydro-Quebec.
exercises.explanation: Jobs need 'an'; company names take no article.

exercises.prompt: The life is too short to work in a job you hate.
answer: Life is too short to work in a job you hate.

exercises.prompt: We met ___ CEO of the company at the conference. (article)
answer: the
exercises.explanation: There is only one CEO of that company → the.

topics.title: Gerunds and Infinitives
topics.summary: Which verbs take -ing, which take to, and which change meaning.
topics.explanation:
+ -ing: avoid, consider, deny, enjoy, finish, mind, postpone, risk, suggest, recommend, look forward to, be used to, object to.
+ to-infinitive: afford, agree, decide, expect, fail, hope, manage, offer, plan, refuse, seem, tend.
Meaning changes: stop doing (quit) vs stop to do (pause in order to); remember doing (memory of past) vs remember to do (not forget a task); try doing (experiment) vs try to do (make an effort); regret to inform (formal bad news) vs regret doing.

After prepositions, always -ing: 'I'm interested in working…', 'Thank you for helping…'. Watch 'to' as a preposition: 'I look forward to hearing from you' (NOT '*to hear').

'Suggest' never takes an object + infinitive: '*He suggested me to apply' → 'He suggested (that) I apply' / 'He suggested applying'.
topics.explanation_fr: « Suggérer à quelqu'un de faire » ne se calque pas : He suggested that I apply. Après une préposition : toujours -ing.

examples.en: I look forward to hearing from you.
We can't afford to lose this client.
Remember to send the minutes.
I remember meeting her in Paris.

exercises.prompt: I'm looking forward to ___ with your team.
The board refused ___ the proposal.
My manager suggested me to take a course.
answer: My manager suggested that I take a course.
My manager suggested I take a course.
My manager suggested taking a course.
My manager suggested that I should take a course.
exercises.explanation: suggest + that-clause or -ing; never object + infinitive.

exercises.prompt: Would you mind ___ (close) the door?
answer: closing

exercises.prompt: He stopped ___ a coffee on the way to work (= paused in order to get one).
exercises.explanation: stop + to = stop in order to do something.

topics.title: Defining and Non-defining Relative Clauses
topics.summary: who, which, that, whose, whom — and where commas change the meaning.
topics.explanation:
Defining clauses identify which one; no commas; 'that' is allowed; the relative pronoun can be dropped if it's the object: 'The analyst (that) we hired is brilliant.'
Non-defining clauses add extra information; commas required; never 'that'; pronoun cannot be dropped: 'Our CFO, who joined in 2020, is retiring.'

'Which' can refer to a whole clause: 'The deal fell through, which surprised everyone.'
'Whose' = possession for people and things: 'a company whose shares doubled'.
'Whom' after prepositions in formal English: 'the person to whom I spoke'.
Prepositions can go at the end informally: 'the person I spoke to'.
topics.explanation_fr: Les virgules changent le sens. Pas de « that » après une virgule. « Dont » se traduit souvent par « whose » ou par une préposition (« the project I told you about »).

examples.en: The report that you sent was very clear.
Toronto, which is Canada's largest city, is a financial hub.
She's the manager whose team won the award.
Prices rose sharply, which hurt consumers.

exercises.prompt: My brother, ___ lives in Calgary, works in oil and gas.
exercises.explanation: Non-defining clause about a person → who (never that).

exercises.prompt: This is the project which I told you.
answer: This is the project I told you about.
This is the project which I told you about.
This is the project that I told you about.
This is the project about which I told you.
exercises.explanation: 'tell someone about something' — the preposition is needed (French 'dont').

exercises.prompt: We partnered with a startup ___ founder used to work at Google.
answer: whose

exercises.prompt: The CEO, that was appointed last year, has resigned.
answer: The CEO, who was appointed last year, has resigned.

topics.title: Reported Speech and Reporting Verbs
topics.summary: Backshift, reported questions, and precise reporting verbs.
topics.explanation:
When the reporting verb is past, tenses usually shift back: 'We are losing money' → She said they were losing money. Present perfect → past perfect; will → would; can → could.
No backshift is needed if the statement is still true: 'He said the office is closed on Mondays.'

Reported questions use statement word order and no question mark: 'Where is the file?' → He asked where the file was (NOT '*where was the file').
Yes/no questions use if/whether.

At C1, replace 'say' with precise verbs: admit, deny, claim, insist, warn, urge, recommend, acknowledge, point out, argue. Note their patterns: deny + -ing, warn sb (not) to, recommend + -ing/that.
topics.explanation_fr: Question rapportée = ordre sujet-verbe, sans inversion ni « do ». « Il m'a demandé où était le dossier » = He asked me where the file was.

examples.en: She told me she had already signed the contract.
He asked whether we could meet on Friday.
The CFO denied manipulating the figures.
The auditor warned us not to delay the filing.

exercises.prompt: She asked me where did I work.
answer: She asked me where I worked.
exercises.explanation: Reported question: statement word order, no 'did'.

exercises.prompt: 'I didn't take the money.' → He ___ taking the money.
exercises.explanation: deny + -ing = say you did not do it.

exercises.prompt: 'Will you be at the meeting?' → She asked ___ I would be at the meeting.
answer: if
whether

exercises.prompt: Report this formally: 'You should diversify your portfolio,' the advisor said to me.
answer: The advisor advised me to diversify my portfolio.
The advisor recommended that I diversify my portfolio.
The advisor recommended diversifying my portfolio.
The advisor advised me to diversify my portfolio
exercises.explanation: advise sb to / recommend that sb (do).

topics.title: Modals of Deduction and Speculation
topics.summary: must, can't, might, could — about the present and the past.
topics.explanation:
Present: must be (almost certain yes), can't be (almost certain no), might/may/could be (possible). 'She must be in a meeting — she's not answering.'
Past: must have + past participle, can't/couldn't have + pp, might/may/could have + pp. 'They must have known about the problem.'

'Mustn't' is NOT the opposite of 'must' for deduction — it means prohibition. Use 'can't' for negative deduction.

Criticism of the past: should have / shouldn't have + pp. 'We should have hedged our currency exposure.'
'Needn't have' = you did it but it wasn't necessary; 'didn't need to' = it wasn't necessary (maybe you didn't do it).
topics.explanation_fr: « Il a dû oublier » = He must have forgotten. « Ça ne peut pas être vrai » = That can't be true (pas « mustn't »). « J'aurais dû » = I should have.

examples.en: The lights are off. They must have gone home.
That can't be the right figure — it's far too high.
The email might have gone to your spam folder.
You needn't have printed the slides; we're using the projector.

exercises.prompt: He looks exhausted. He ___ worked all night.
She ___ be the new director — she only joined last week as an intern.
Traduisez : « On aurait dû vendre nos actions en janvier. »
answer: We should have sold our shares in January.
We should have sold our stocks in January.
exercises.explanation: Regret/criticism about the past → should have + pp.

exercises.prompt: He must forgot the password.
answer: He must have forgotten the password.
exercises.explanation: Past deduction: must have + past participle.

topics.title: The Subjunctive and Unreal Past
topics.summary: It's essential that he be…; I wish I had…; It's time we left.
topics.explanation:
Mandative subjunctive (formal, very common in US and Canadian business English): after verbs/adjectives of demand or importance, use the base form for all persons: 'The board insists that the CEO resign.' 'It is essential that every employee complete the training.' British English often uses 'should': 'that every employee should complete…'.

Unreal past: after wish, if only, would rather, it's (high) time, as if — use past for present meaning and past perfect for past meaning:
'I wish I spoke better English.' (present regret)
'I wish I had studied harder.' (past regret)
'It's high time we updated our systems.'
'I'd rather you didn't share this.'

'Wish + would' is for complaints about others' behaviour: 'I wish they would reply.'
topics.explanation_fr: Le subjonctif anglais = forme de base sans -s : « Il est indispensable qu'il soit présent » = It is essential that he be present.

examples.en: We recommend that the company diversify its revenue streams.
If only I had accepted that offer!
It's time we made a decision.
She talks as if she were the owner.

exercises.prompt: The regulator demanded that the bank ___ its reserves.
I wish I ___ (have) more time to prepare for the interview yesterday.
answer: had had

exercises.prompt: It's time we leave.
answer: It's time we left.
It is time we left.
It's time for us to leave.
It's time to leave.

exercises.prompt: I would rather you don't tell anyone.
answer: I would rather you didn't tell anyone.
I'd rather you didn't tell anyone.

topics.title: Cleft Sentences for Emphasis
topics.summary: It was… that…; What I need is…; The reason why… is…
topics.explanation:
Cleft sentences split one idea into two clauses to highlight the important part — essential for presentations and persuasive speaking.

It-cleft: It + be + focus + that/who: 'It was the marketing team that found the error.' 'It's not the price that worries me, it's the timeline.'
Wh-cleft: What + clause + be + focus: 'What we need is a clear strategy.' 'What I'd like to do is (to) walk you through the numbers.'
Other patterns: 'All I want is…', 'The thing that surprised me was…', 'The reason (why) we chose them is that…' (not '*is because').
topics.explanation_fr: Équivalent de « C'est … qui/que » et « Ce dont nous avons besoin, c'est… ». Très utile pour structurer une présentation orale.

examples.en: What really matters is the long-term return.
It was in 2008 that the crisis really began.
What I'd like to do now is look at the risks.
The reason we're late is that the train broke down.

exercises.prompt: Emphasise 'a better work-life balance': 'We need a better work-life balance.'
answer: What we need is a better work-life balance.
What we need is a better work–life balance.
It's a better work-life balance that we need.
It is a better work-life balance that we need.
exercises.explanation: Wh-cleft: What + subject + verb + is + focus.

exercises.prompt: It was the CFO ___ approved the budget.
exercises.explanation: It-cleft focusing on a person → who/that.

exercises.prompt: The reason why I applied is because I love finance.
answer: The reason why I applied is that I love finance.
The reason I applied is that I love finance.
I applied because I love finance.
exercises.explanation: 'The reason … is that' (avoid 'is because' in formal English).

topics.title: Dependent Prepositions (French Interference)
topics.summary: The prepositions French speakers most often get wrong.
topics.explanation:
Many English verbs, adjectives and nouns require a fixed preposition that differs from French:
- depend ON (not *of) — dépendre de
- married TO (not *with) — marié avec
- responsible FOR — responsable de
- good AT (skill) — bon en
- arrive IN a city / AT a place (never *arrive to)
- interested IN, specialise IN
- discuss sth (no preposition: *discuss about) — discuter de
- explain sth TO sb (not *explain me) — m'expliquer
- listen TO, wait FOR, ask FOR, pay FOR
- the reason FOR, an increase IN, the key TO, the solution TO
- on the phone, on the internet, at the weekend (UK) / on the weekend (US/CA)
topics.explanation_fr: Ces erreurs viennent du calque du français. Apprenez le verbe avec sa préposition comme un seul bloc.

examples.en: It depends on the interest rate.
Could you explain the process to me?
We discussed the budget.
There has been a sharp increase in demand.

exercises.prompt: Can you explain me the difference?
answer: Can you explain the difference to me?
Could you explain the difference to me?

exercises.prompt: We need to discuss about the contract.
answer: We need to discuss the contract.
We need to talk about the contract.

exercises.prompt: It depends ___ the market conditions.
We arrived ___ Toronto at midnight.
She's married ___ a lawyer.
answer: to

topics.title: Future Forms: will, going to, present continuous
topics.summary: Choose the right future for decisions, plans, arrangements, predictions and schedules.
topics.explanation:
will: decisions made at the moment of speaking, promises, offers, and predictions based on opinion. 'I'll send it right away.' 'I think rates will fall.'
going to: plans already decided, and predictions based on present evidence. 'We're going to hire two analysts.' 'Look at those clouds — it's going to rain.'
Present continuous: fixed personal arrangements, usually with a time. 'I'm meeting the CFO on Thursday.'
Present simple: timetables and schedules. 'The flight leaves at 7:15.'
Future continuous (will be + -ing): an action in progress at a future time, or a polite question about plans. 'This time tomorrow I'll be flying to Calgary.' 'Will you be using the meeting room?'
Future perfect (will have + pp): completed before a future time. 'By June we will have launched the product.'
No 'will' after when/as soon as/before/until/if in future time clauses: 'I'll call you when I arrive' (NOT *when I will arrive).
topics.explanation_fr: Après « when, as soon as, before, until », présent en anglais (là où le français met un futur) : « Je t'appellerai quand j'arriverai » = I'll call you when I arrive.

examples.en: I'm seeing the dentist at four.
By the end of the year, we'll have doubled our client base.
I'll let you know as soon as I hear anything.
The market opens at 9:30.

exercises.prompt: I'll call you as soon as I ___ the results.
exercises.explanation: No 'will' in a future time clause.

exercises.prompt: The phone's ringing. — Don't worry, I ___ it.
exercises.explanation: Decision at the moment of speaking → will.

exercises.prompt: By the time you arrive, we ___ (finish) the presentation.
answer: will have finished
'll have finished
exercises.explanation: Completed before a future moment → future perfect.

exercises.prompt: When I will finish my MBA, I will look for a job in Toronto.
answer: When I finish my MBA, I will look for a job in Toronto.
When I finish my MBA, I'll look for a job in Toronto.
When I have finished my MBA, I will look for a job in Toronto.
exercises.explanation: Present tense after 'when' for future time.

exercises.prompt: This time next week I ___ on a beach in Cuba.
exercises.explanation: Action in progress at a future moment → future continuous.

topics.title: Subject–Verb Agreement
topics.summary: Tricky subjects: collective nouns, 'each', 'the number of', uncountables and long noun phrases.
topics.explanation:
The verb agrees with the head noun, not the nearest noun: 'The quality of the reports IS excellent.'
Each / every / either / neither + singular: 'Each of the candidates HAS a CV.' ('Neither… nor' agrees with the nearer subject.)
'The number of' + singular; 'a number of' + plural: 'The number of applicants HAS risen.' 'A number of applicants HAVE withdrawn.'
Uncountables are singular: information, advice, news, research, equipment, feedback, evidence: 'The news IS good.' (NOT *the news are; NOT *informations, *advices)
Collective nouns (team, staff, government, company): singular in North American English, singular or plural in British English. 'The team is…' (US/CA) / 'The team are…' (UK).
Amounts of money/time/distance are singular: 'Ten million dollars IS a lot.'
'People', 'police', 'staff' (CA/US often singular for staff) — 'people' is always plural: 'People ARE…'.
topics.explanation_fr: Attention aux indénombrables : information, advice, news, research, feedback ne prennent jamais de -s et sont au singulier.

examples.en: The results of the survey are encouraging.
Neither the manager nor the employees were informed.
Your feedback has been very useful.
Five years is a long time to wait.

exercises.prompt: The list of items ___ on the desk.
Thank you for all the informations and advices.
answer: Thank you for all the information and advice.

exercises.prompt: The number of complaints ___ fallen this year.
Each of the analysts ___ (be) responsible for one sector.
answer: is

exercises.prompt: The news are very worrying for investors.
answer: The news is very worrying for investors.

topics.title: Participle Clauses
topics.summary: Compress information elegantly with -ing, -ed and having + past participle.
topics.explanation:
Participle clauses replace a subject + verb in a subordinate clause, making writing more concise and formal.
Present participle (-ing) — active, simultaneous or reason: 'Feeling unwell, she left the meeting early.' (= Because she felt unwell)
Past participle (-ed) — passive meaning: 'Founded in 1867, the bank is one of Canada's oldest.' (= which was founded)
Perfect participle (having + pp) — one action completed before another: 'Having reviewed the data, the committee approved the loan.'
Reduced relative clauses: 'The candidates shortlisted for the role will be contacted.' 'Anyone wishing to attend should register.'
The subject of the participle clause MUST be the same as the main clause; otherwise you get a 'dangling participle': '*Walking into the office, the computer was on.' (The computer wasn't walking!) → 'Walking into the office, I saw that the computer was on.'
topics.explanation_fr: Le sujet implicite du participe doit être celui de la principale. « Ayant terminé le rapport, je l'ai envoyé » = Having finished the report, I sent it.

examples.en: Having worked in banking for ten years, he understands risk well.
Written in plain English, the guide is easy to follow.
Not knowing what to say, I remained silent.
Employees working remotely must use the VPN.

exercises.prompt: ___ the contract, they started the project immediately.
exercises.explanation: Completed earlier action, active → having + pp.

exercises.prompt: ___ in 1990, the company now employs 5,000 people.
Arriving late, the meeting had already started.
answer: Arriving late, I found that the meeting had already started.
Arriving late, we found that the meeting had already started.
When I arrived late, the meeting had already started.
When I arrived, the meeting had already started.
exercises.explanation: Dangling participle: the meeting didn't arrive late.

exercises.prompt: Combine with a participle clause: 'She didn't know the answer. She asked her colleague.'
answer: Not knowing the answer, she asked her colleague.

topics.title: Noun Clauses (that, wh-, whether)
topics.summary: Clauses that act as subjects or objects: 'What surprised me was…', 'Whether we succeed depends on…'.
topics.explanation:
A noun clause does the job of a noun: subject, object or complement.
that-clauses: 'I believe (that) the plan will work.' As subject, 'that' is required and often replaced by 'It… that': 'That the CEO resigned surprised no one.' → 'It surprised no one that the CEO resigned.'
wh-clauses use statement word order: 'I don't know where the file is.' (NOT *where is the file) 'What matters is the result.'
whether/if-clauses for yes/no: 'Whether we expand depends on funding.' Use 'whether' (not 'if') as subject, after prepositions and before 'to': 'We discussed whether to hire.'
'The fact that' allows a that-clause after prepositions: 'Despite the fact that sales fell…' (NOT *despite that sales fell).
topics.explanation_fr: « Ce que » = what : « Ce qui compte, c'est… » = What matters is… Ordre affirmatif dans les subordonnées interrogatives.

examples.en: What we need is more time.
It's unclear whether the merger will be approved.
Could you tell me where the conference room is?
Despite the fact that rates rose, demand stayed strong.

exercises.prompt: Can you tell me where is the nearest bank?
answer: Can you tell me where the nearest bank is?

exercises.prompt: ___ we can meet the deadline depends on the supplier.
Traduisez : « Ce qui m'inquiète, c'est le coût. »
answer: What worries me is the cost.
What concerns me is the cost.

exercises.prompt: Despite that the market fell, our fund grew.
answer: Despite the fact that the market fell, our fund grew.
Although the market fell, our fund grew.
Even though the market fell, our fund grew.
exercises.explanation: 'despite' is a preposition: use 'the fact that' or switch to 'although'.

topics.title: Punctuation for Professional Writing
topics.summary: Commas, semicolons, colons, apostrophes, and avoiding comma splices.
topics.explanation:
Comma splice: two complete sentences joined with only a comma are wrong in English (they are common in French). '*Sales rose, profits fell.' Fix with a full stop, a semicolon, or a conjunction: 'Sales rose, but profits fell.' / 'Sales rose; profits fell.'
Semicolon (;) joins closely related independent clauses, especially before 'however', 'therefore', 'moreover': 'Costs increased; however, margins held.'
Colon (:) introduces a list, explanation or example after a complete clause: 'We have one priority: growth.'
Commas after introductory phrases ('In 2025, …'), around non-defining clauses, and before 'but/so/yet' joining clauses. No comma before a that-clause: 'He said that…' (NOT *He said, that…).
Apostrophes: possession ('the company's results', 'the companies' results') and contractions. 'its' (possessive) vs 'it's' (it is).
No space before ? ! : ; in English (unlike French).
topics.explanation_fr: En anglais : pas d'espace avant « ; : ? ! », pas de virgule entre deux phrases complètes, et « however » se ponctue « ; however, ».

examples.en: The project was delayed; however, the budget was respected.
Three markets grew: Canada, Mexico and Brazil.
The bank raised its rates.
Prices fell, so demand increased.

exercises.prompt: The meeting was long, nobody reached a decision.
answer: The meeting was long, but nobody reached a decision.
The meeting was long; nobody reached a decision.
The meeting was long. Nobody reached a decision.
The meeting was long, and nobody reached a decision.
The meeting was long, yet nobody reached a decision.
exercises.explanation: Comma splice: use a conjunction, semicolon or full stop.

exercises.prompt: The company announced ___ quarterly results.
Revenue grew however costs grew faster.
answer: Revenue grew; however, costs grew faster.
Revenue grew. However, costs grew faster.
exercises.explanation: 'however' between clauses needs ; or . and a comma after.

exercises.prompt: Which is correctly punctuated in English?
exercises.explanation: No space before a question mark in English.

topics.title: Hedging and Academic Caution
topics.summary: Sound credible by qualifying your claims: may, appears to, tends to, it could be argued that.
topics.explanation:
Academic and professional English avoids absolute claims that the evidence cannot support. Hedging shows precision, not weakness.
Modal verbs: may, might, could ('This may reflect…').
Lexical verbs: appear to, seem to, tend to, suggest, indicate ('The data suggest that…').
Adverbs: possibly, arguably, largely, broadly, to some extent, in most cases.
Impersonal structures: It could be argued that…, It is likely that…, There is some evidence that…
Quantifiers instead of absolutes: 'many/most' instead of 'all', 'often' instead of 'always'.
Boosters, used sparingly when evidence is strong: clearly, undoubtedly, demonstrates.
Avoid over-hedging: '*It might possibly perhaps suggest…' is weak.
topics.explanation_fr: Équivalent de « il semblerait que », « dans une certaine mesure ». En IELTS/rédaction académique, les affirmations nuancées sont mieux notées.

examples.en: These findings suggest that remote work may increase productivity.
It could be argued that the policy was introduced too early.
Inflation appears to have peaked.
Social media is, to some extent, responsible for polarisation.

exercises.prompt: Which sentence is most appropriately hedged for an academic essay?
options: Technology may displace some jobs while creating others.
Technology definitely has no effect on jobs.
exercises.answer: Technology may displace some jobs while creating others.

exercises.prompt: Hedge this claim: 'Higher taxes reduce investment.'
answer: Higher taxes may reduce investment.
Higher taxes tend to reduce investment.
Higher taxes can reduce investment.
Higher taxes might reduce investment.
Higher taxes could reduce investment.
Higher taxes appear to reduce investment.
Higher taxes may tend to reduce investment.

exercises.prompt: The results ___ to indicate a link between sleep and memory. (verb: seem/appear)
answer: seem
appear

exercises.prompt: Choose the over-hedged sentence:
options: The data may indicate a trend.
It could perhaps possibly be suggested that there might be a trend.
There appears to be a trend.
exercises.answer: It could perhaps possibly be suggested that there might be a trend.

topics.title: Nominalisation
topics.summary: Turn verbs and adjectives into nouns for dense, formal, written English.
topics.explanation:
Nominalisation means expressing processes as nouns: 'Prices increased rapidly, which worried investors' → 'The rapid increase in prices worried investors.'
It makes writing more concise, objective and cohesive, because a noun phrase can become the subject of the next sentence: 'The government cut spending. This reduction…'
Common patterns: verb → noun (analyse → analysis, fail → failure, decide → decision, reduce → reduction, grow → growth), adjective → noun (stable → stability, available → availability, important → importance).
Watch the prepositions: an increase IN, a decline IN, a reduction IN/OF, the analysis OF, the failure TO do / OF something, a decision TO do / ON something.
Overuse creates heavy, unclear prose ('the implementation of the facilitation of…'). Use it in reports and essays; keep speech and emails more verbal.
topics.explanation_fr: Typique de l'écrit académique, comme en français (« l'augmentation des prix » plutôt que « les prix ont augmenté »).

examples.en: The failure of the merger led to job losses.
There has been a significant decline in demand.
The availability of credit is essential for growth.
Their decision to withdraw surprised analysts.

exercises.prompt: Nominalise: 'The company expanded quickly, and this attracted investors.'
answer: The company's rapid expansion attracted investors.
The rapid expansion of the company attracted investors.
The company's quick expansion attracted investors.

exercises.prompt: There has been a sharp ___ unemployment.
Nominalise: 'Because the economy is unstable, firms delay investment.'
answer: The instability of the economy causes firms to delay investment.
Economic instability causes firms to delay investment.
Due to economic instability, firms delay investment.
Because of economic instability, firms delay investment.
Economic instability leads firms to delay investment.

exercises.prompt: The ___ (analyse) of the data took three weeks.
answer: analysis

topics.title: Ellipsis and Substitution
topics.summary: Avoid repetition like a native speaker: so, not, one(s), do so, and leaving words out.
topics.explanation:
Native speakers rarely repeat whole phrases. They substitute or omit.
Substitution: one/ones for countable nouns ('I prefer the blue one'); do/does/did for verb phrases ('She works harder than I do'); do so in formal style ('The board was asked to reconsider, and it did so'); so/not for clauses after think, hope, expect, suppose, be afraid ('Will rates rise? — I expect so / I hope not').
Ellipsis (leaving out words recoverable from context): after auxiliaries ('I haven't finished, but Sarah has.'), after 'to' ('I'd like to come, but I'm not able to.'), in comparisons ('He earns more than I.' formal / 'than me' informal), and in coordinated clauses ('Some invested in stocks, others in bonds.').
French speakers often say '*I think yes' (je pense que oui) → 'I think so'; '*I hope' alone → 'I hope so'.
topics.explanation_fr: « Je pense que oui / non » = I think so / I don't think so. « J'espère » en réponse = I hope so.

examples.en: Will the deal close this week? — I don't think so.
You said you'd call, but you didn't.
Is the report ready? — I'm afraid not.
Applicants were invited to resubmit, and many did so.

exercises.prompt: Is she coming to the conference? — I think yes.
answer: I think so.
I think so
Is she coming to the conference? — I think so.

exercises.prompt: Are prices going to rise again? — I hope ___.
exercises.explanation: hope not = I hope they won't.

exercises.prompt: I wanted to attend the webinar, but I wasn't able ___.
answer: to

exercises.prompt: These reports are better than the ___ we received last year.

topics.title: Quantifiers and Determiners
topics.summary: much/many, few/a few, little/a little, each/every, either/neither, all/whole.
topics.explanation:
Countable plural: many, (a) few, fewer, a number of. Uncountable: much, (a) little, less, an amount of. Both: a lot of, plenty of, some, any, no, most.
'A few / a little' = some (positive); 'few / little' = not enough (negative): 'Few candidates passed' (disappointing) vs 'A few candidates passed' (some did).
'Each' looks at members individually (often two or more); 'every' at the whole group (three or more): 'Each partner signed.' 'Every employee received a bonus.'
'Either/neither' for two: 'Neither option is ideal.' 'All' vs 'whole': 'all the day' is unnatural → 'the whole day', 'all day'.
In formal English, use 'fewer' with countables: 'fewer errors' (not *less errors).
topics.explanation_fr: « Peu de » = few/little ; « quelques » = a few. « Moins de » + dénombrable = fewer.

examples.en: We received fewer complaints this quarter.
There's little evidence to support the claim.
Each of the three options has drawbacks.
I spent the whole afternoon on the report.

exercises.prompt: There were ___ questions after the talk, so we finished early.
We have ___ time left: let's take a short break.
There were less people at the conference than last year.
answer: There were fewer people at the conference than last year.

exercises.prompt: ___ of the two proposals was accepted; both were rejected.
I worked all the day on the presentation.
answer: I worked all day on the presentation.
I worked the whole day on the presentation.

topics.title: Causatives: have/get something done
topics.summary: Arranging for others to do things, and 'have/get someone do/to do'.
topics.explanation:
have/get + object + past participle = arrange for someone else to do it: 'We had the accounts audited.' 'I need to get my laptop repaired.'
Also for unpleasant experiences: 'He had his wallet stolen.'
have + person + infinitive (without to): 'I'll have my assistant send you the file.'
get + person + to-infinitive (persuade): 'I got the bank to waive the fee.'
make + person + infinitive (force): 'They made us sign a confidentiality agreement.'
let + person + infinitive (allow): 'My manager let me work from home.'
topics.explanation_fr: « Faire faire » = have/get something done : « J'ai fait réparer ma voiture » = I had my car repaired.

topics.title: Future in the Past
topics.summary: was going to, would, was about to, was to: talking about the future from a past viewpoint.
topics.explanation:
Use these forms to describe what was planned, expected or predicted at a past moment.
was/were going to: plans that often did not happen: 'I was going to call you, but I forgot.'
would: predictions/reported futures: 'She knew the project would succeed.'
was/were about to: something on the point of happening: 'We were about to sign when the deal collapsed.'
was/were to (formal): destiny or arrangements: 'He was to become CEO ten years later.' 'The meeting was to have taken place on Monday' (but didn't).
was/were (just) on the point of + -ing: 'I was on the point of leaving.'
topics.explanation_fr: « J'allais t'appeler » = I was going to call you. « Il allait devenir PDG » (destin) = He was to become CEO.

examples.en: I was going to apply, but the deadline had passed.
Nobody imagined the company would grow so fast.
They were about to launch when the regulator intervened.
Little did she know she was to lead the firm one day.

topics.title: Discourse Markers for Speaking and Writing
topics.summary: however, nevertheless, whereas, as a result, that said, admittedly: linking ideas precisely.
topics.explanation:
Contrast: however, nevertheless, nonetheless (formal, sentence-linking); whereas, while (contrast two clauses); that said / having said that (spoken, concession after a point); even so.
Concession: admittedly, granted, it is true that… but…
Cause/result: as a result, consequently, therefore, thus (formal), hence (formal, often + noun: 'hence the delay').
Addition: moreover, furthermore, in addition, what is more.
Reformulation: in other words, that is to say, to put it another way.
Punctuation: 'However' joining clauses needs a semicolon or full stop: 'Sales rose; however, costs rose faster.' 'Whereas' joins clauses directly: 'Sales rose, whereas costs fell.'
French traps: 'actually' ≠ actuellement (= currently); 'eventually' ≠ éventuellement (= possibly); 'in fact' is fine; 'at the contrary' → 'on the contrary'.
topics.explanation_fr: Faux amis : « actually » = en fait ; « eventually » = finalement ; « éventuellement » = possibly ; « au contraire » = on the contrary.

examples.en: The plan is ambitious. That said, it is achievable.
Prices rose sharply; hence the drop in demand.
Admittedly, the data are limited, but the trend is clear.
Currently, we have two offices.
